sections.title: 1. The Customer Problem and Discovery
sections.text: 1. The Customer Problem and DiscoveryReframing the Request The room agrees on the headline, "one platform for similar workflows", and on little else. Fields, approval paths, audit depth and release process all differ by stakeholder. Don't start by drawing services. First turn the vague ask into a measurable outcome: one configurable workflow platform on which ten customers can each change their fields, approvals, branding and integrations, while the shared core stays stable, versioned and supportable. Separate the feature someone asked for ("configuration") from the result the business needs: each customer gets its own workflow, and the product does not splinter into ten forks that cannot talk to each other. Say that split aloud; an implementer skips it, an FDE (Forward Deployed Engineer) leads with it. Make each word in the outcome testable: Safe: no change can skip authorisation or switch on runtime behaviour that nobody reviewed. Versioned: every customer can see which workflow definition is live and what changed in it. Supportable: support and release staff can trace a fault, undo a bad configuration and explain behaviour tenant by tenant. Avoid vanity measures such as the number of configurable fields. Track how often a new customer variation ships with no fork, no hotfix and no support escalation. Frame it as a job to be done: the customer hires the platform to make custom forks unnecessary while each tenant keeps its own process. That pushes the design towards a stable core with a few controlled extension points instead of a codebase that changes shape per account. Interview pointer: Learn the outcome statement by heart: "keep one stable product core, and allow customisation that is safe, versioned and supportable." Interviewers listen for those three words, because each one drives a later architecture decision. Stakeholder Map One request means something different to each group: Customer administrators ask who may change a workflow, how much they may customise, and how fast a change reaches users. FDE teams want a real customer use case in production without leaving one-off code behind. Core platform engineers want a lasting model for workflow definitions, validation, permissions and how the runtime executes them. Support and release teams want observability, rollback, a clear incident process and a quick answer to "what changed?" Drop a group and the design tilts: without support you ship flexibility nobody can operate; without platform engineers the customer layer never generalises. The concrete map, one line per role: End user: a customer employee who starts a workflow, approves it, or is on the receiving end of its result. Operator: on the support or release team; watches health, reverts a bad config, handles incidents. Security owner: answers for permissions, audit and least privilege between tenants. Executive sponsor: the business leader paying for one platform rollout instead of a run of forks and long customisation projects. Discovery Question Tree Time is short, so skip the twenty generic questions. Ask the few that remove the most doubt. Workflow shape: Which parts are the same for every customer, and which really differ? Is the variation only in fields, routing, branding and integrations, or does it also touch business logic and lifecycle states? Ownership and control: Who may write configuration changes, and who signs them off? Do customer admins change configuration themselves, or does an FDE or platform team handle every change? Risk and recovery: What happens when someone misconfigures a workflow? Can the customer live with a broken approval path, or must a fallback always exist? Success: What counts as "done" for the first customer: one live workflow, several teams onboarded, or every variation migrated? How will the customer judge it: less manual handling, faster turnaround, fewer errors or simpler audits? The answers become the design's inputs: scope, assumptions, risks, owners and success measures. If the interviewer holds back, state your assumption aloud: "I'll assume only customer admins can configure, and the vendor approves each change before production." That sets a clear boundary. Assumption Ledger A useful discovery pass leaves four things on the table: Scope: what is configurable and what stays fixed. Assumptions: what you accept for now because the prompt left it open. Risks: where a bad configuration, a permission slip or a failed integration could hurt a customer. Success criteria: the measurable change that shows the platform works. Weak vs. Strong Answers A weak restatement leads with features: "Let's build a flexible workflow system: forms, approvals, themes and some API hooks." A strong restatement leads with the outcome: "We need a single shared workflow platform. Each customer can tailor its fields, approvals, branding and integrations without a separate codebase, and the core stays stable enough to version, support and roll out safely." The second version names the tension between flexibility and fragmentation. A short spoken opening: "Let me frame it first. One workflow product, ten customers, each wanting its own fields, approval chains, branding and integrations. I want a stable shared core with safe, versioned, supportable customisation, so we never run ten forks. First I'd find out who owns configuration, which variations are really needed, which failures we can't accept, and how we'll measure the first rollout. Then the design rests on validation, rollback and a few controlled extension points, not per-customer code." It works because it names the problem and the people, and holds the architecture back until someone owns the workflow, someone owns the risk and a success metric exists.

sections.title: 2. Clarifying Questions, Requirements, and Constraints
sections.text: 2. Clarifying Questions, Requirements, and ConstraintsRequirement vs. Preference Don't take "we need flexibility" at face value, or you lose control of the design. Ask who needs it, under what governance, and with what promise about upgrades. Sort requirements from preferences and hard constraints from conveniences. Every customer wants a slightly different mix of fields, approvals, branding, integrations and sometimes rules. The first design fork is spotting which differences repeat. Skip that, along with who authors configuration and where custom code ends, and you get one of two failures: a platform that is too thin, or a bespoke rules engine nobody can support safely. The Six-Question Interview Tree Six questions keep the conversation away from a feature wish list: Which differences keep coming back between customers? This separates a shared product pattern from one-offs. Approval chains that differ again and again are a platform capability; one seasonal override goes down an exception path. It also tells you what the core abstraction is: steps, policy rules, form schemas or integration orchestration. Who will write the configuration? This is an architecture question. Internal engineers can handle expressive power; customer admins and support staff need guardrails such as validation, previews, narrow building blocks and safe defaults. The answer reshapes the UX, the validation model and the authorisation model. Which integrations and extensions can't be dropped? Typical items are webhook callbacks, outbound notifications, CRM (customer relationship management) sync, document generation, ticket creation and auth hooks. The list fixes the adapter interface, settles sync versus async, and decides whether a failed call blocks a transition or degrades gracefully. What upgrade promise do customers expect? If configs must outlive core releases, you need versioning, migration tooling, backward-compatible schema changes and rollback paths. Without them the "product core" becomes an endless services project. Where does the security boundary for custom code sit? Options are the trusted core itself, a sandbox, or approved integration points only. The choice sets tenant isolation and supply-chain scrutiny. Default to a declarative core, with arbitrary code kept beyond the main trust boundary. How fast must a configuration change go live? Changes needed within hours call for self-service tooling with validation built in. A week allows more manual review. The target decides where you invest: admin UX, reusable templates, automated testing or partner onboarding. Interview pointer: Expect follow-ups on question 5, the custom-code boundary. Have the default ready (a declarative core, with any arbitrary code kept outside the trust boundary) and link it to the sandbox component in the architecture section and the controls in the security section. Must-Have Functional Requirements A stable workflow engine that runs one core lifecycle for all customers. Declarative configuration (schemas, rules, UI metadata) for labels, fields, visibility and validation, so no customer needs a code fork. An adapter interface, so external systems plug in and the engine stays untouched. Versioned configuration with validation, so every change can be reviewed, tested and reverted. A small set of controlled extension points for the rare cases declarative configuration cannot cover. Migration and rollback tooling, so a version change never strands a customer on an incompatible config. How they fit: the engine is the centre, so there is one release train, one way to operate and one thing to support. Most variation lives in declarative configuration, not code. Integrations go through the adapter interface instead of each becoming a special case. Versioning and validation make customisation supportable. Extension points stay narrow and explicit, never a blank cheque. Measurable Non-Functional Requirements One core release train: a single product ships, never ten customer branches. Configuration isolation: no customer's settings, data or test changes can leak into how another customer's workflows run. Backward-compatible upgrades: an existing configuration keeps working until a planned migration runs. Observable customer-specific behaviour: when a workflow goes wrong, operators can see the config version involved and which rule or adapter fired. Each one shapes the system. No observability means no support. No backward compatibility turns configuration into a liability. Weak isolation turns customisation into a steady stream of multi-tenant incidents. MVP Non-Goals / Scope Fence The MVP (minimum viable product) leaves out: Code written by customers and run inside the workflow engine. Endless per-customer UI branches to meet branding requests. A general-purpose rules language that tries to model any business process. Bespoke integration behaviour that goes around the adapter contract. Automatic, unreviewed migration of every legacy configuration shape. These cuts protect the core. The MVP proves that one platform can serve ten customers with safe variation, not that it can model every workflow on day one. Requirement-to-Component Traceability Give every requirement a likely home: Requirement Likely component Stable workflow engine Workflow runtime / orchestrator Declarative schemas, rules, UI metadata Config model, schema registry, admin UI Adapter interface for integrations Integration gateway / connector layer Versioned configuration and validation Config service, validator, release pipeline Controlled extension points Sandbox or plugin boundary Migration and rollback tooling Deployment and ops tooling One core release train Shared platform build and release process Configuration isolation Tenant-aware data and authorisation layer Backward-compatible upgrades Schema evolution and compatibility checks Observable customer-specific behaviour Audit logs, metrics, tracing, config-version tags Handling Partial Answers If only some questions get answers, don't stall. Assume sensibly and guard the riskiest constraint. Say the customers look alike but nobody says who authors configuration. Assume a mix: the customer's admins own the safe declarative fields, and our ops team signs off any extension or schema change. That guards the most fragile line, between safe customisation and unsafe code. This tests discovery under ambiguity, prioritisation with gaps, and the habit of protecting delivery by narrowing scope. The Strong Candidate Move The strong move runs in order: find the recurring differences, settle who owns configuration, state the integration and upgrade promise, draw a firm line for custom code, then commit to a stable engine backed by declarative configuration, versioning and strict validation. That order turns discovery into a buildable plan. Ask only questions that change the design, then proceed on stated assumptions.

Requirement Likely component

sections.text: 4. Architecture and End-to-End FlowControl Plane vs. Data Plane To present this system, follow one tenant request end to end, then replay it with a dependency in poor health. A customer's own approval logic becomes dangerous if it can change how the shared runtime behaves. So the design has two halves. The control plane is where configuration gets written, checked, versioned and promoted. The data plane runs live workflow instances. Keeping them apart moves risky change management off the hot path. Control plane duties: editing configs, checking schemas, running tenant contract tests, promoting releases. Data plane duties: workflow execution, runtime UI rendering, connector calls and audit events. If asked where the trust boundary sits, point at this split first. Architecture Diagram and Trust Boundaries Read the diagram top to bottom. A tenant's change request enters the control plane. It passes the config editor, then the schema/rule validator and tenant test harness, then the configuration registry (the system of record), then the feature flag service that gates exposure. The data plane follows: workflow runtime, UI renderer, integration adapter SDK, and approved extensions in a sandbox. External systems sit last: customer APIs, the identity provider and notification services. There are two trust boundaries. One lies between content a tenant writes and execution the platform owns. The other lies between platform execution and outside dependencies. Config written by a tenant never runs as code with full platform trust. Even approved extensions stay untrusted enough to need isolation and quotas. You do not control external systems. Give every adapter call timeouts, retries, idempotency where it applies, and a backoff policy that does not make a failure worse. Core Components in Dependency Order The table lists the components in dependency order. Component Responsibility State ownership Typical boundary Workflow runtime Runs workflow instances, moves between steps, fires timers and retries Execution history, runtime state Data plane; step decisions are synchronous, long-running work is asynchronous Configuration registry Keeps every config and schema version with its release metadata Immutable config versions Control plane; the system of record once a config is published Schema and rule validator Verifies syntax, semantic rules, permissions and compatibility Only its check results Control plane; blocks on save/publish UI renderer Turns approved config into each tenant's forms, labels and layouts Cache only Mostly data plane; renders synchronously from cached descriptors Integration adapter SDK A common contract for webhook, ticketing, ERP and CRM adapters Adapter definitions, credentials references Data plane edge facing external systems Feature flag service Controls rollout per tenant, cohort or percentage Flag state Spans both planes Sandbox for approved extensions Executes tightly scoped customer logic or plugins under hard limits Ephemeral execution only Isolated; synchronous when small, async otherwise Migration service Upgrades older configs to new schema versions, or moves instances forward Migration jobs, compatibility mappings Control plane; mostly asynchronous Tenant test harness Re-runs each tenant's contract tests ahead of release Test fixtures, expected outcomes Control plane; a synchronous approval gate or an async batch The validator keeps junk out of the registry. The flag service exists because publishing a version and showing it to every tenant are two different actions. The sandbox exists because approved extensions are valuable, yet letting arbitrary code run at runtime is how customisation ends in incident response. Failure-Path Overlay: Infinite Approval Loop This overlay marks up the architecture for the infinite-approval-loop failure drill to show the blast radius. The validator, the test harness and the flags each shrink it at a separate stage. If one layer misses the defect, a later one still prevents a tenant-wide incident. Happy-Path Sequence: Author to Promotion The live release path, one step at a time: Author config against a versioned schema. A customer admin, an implementation engineer or a product manager edits the workflow definition, approval graph, field layout and adapter mappings. Validate syntax and semantic constraints. Checks cover structure, permitted field types, whether the approval graph makes sense, reference integrity, permissions, and fit with the features switched on. Run tenant contract tests. The harness replays typical scenarios: form submission, approval routing, odd edge inputs and integration stubs. Publish an immutable version. The registry keeps that precise artifact plus its version tag, schema version, release metadata and who wrote it, so it records exactly what was approved. Roll out behind a tenant flag. One tenant sees it first, then a cohort, then wider traffic once it proves stable. Observe behaviour. Watch step latency, failed validations, adapter errors, approval-loop detection and how often users finish the workflow. Promote or rollback. A release that clears the acceptance gate goes active. A release that fails has its flag switched back, or its tenant stays pinned to the earlier immutable version. Publishing a version and switching it on everywhere are separate steps. Keeping them apart stops one bad config from causing a wide outage. Some steps should block and some should not. Validation and contract tests are synchronous gates, because they must hold back promotion. Bulk replay, migration and some integration recovery suit async work, so the user's request does not stay open. The runtime usually does both: quick step decisions inline, and external side effects pushed to async work when a dependency is slow or flaky. Systems of Record, Caches, Queues, and Backpressure System of record: published versions belong to the configuration registry; execution history normally belongs to the workflow audit store. Caches: recent flag decisions, adapter metadata, form layouts once rendered, and compiled schema descriptors. Queues: test harness batches, migration tasks, event delivery, retries and adapter jobs. Backpressure and flow control: as adapter queues grow, the runtime should drop or defer noncritical work instead of letting retries stampede external systems. The partitioning key is normally tenant ID, sometimes paired with workflow definition ID or environment. It stops a noisy tenant from spoiling latency for the rest, makes replay easier, and gives quotas an obvious place to be enforced. A surge of approvals from one tenant should stay inside its partition. MVP vs. Later Evolution For the MVP (minimum viable product), stay ruthlessly simple: the runtime, a versioned registry, the validator, feature flags, the tenant test harness, a small adapter SDK, and only as much sandbox as approved extensions strictly need. Prefer immutable config versions and an obvious rollback over a fancier live-editing system. Leave for later: config templates shared across tenants, more automated migration, a wider plugin marketplace and deeper visibility into tenant behaviour. Add them once the core release path is stable and easy to support. 90-Second Interview Summary "I'd split the system into two planes. The control plane is where people write configs, where schemas and rules get checked, where tenant contract tests run, and where versions are frozen and rolled out with feature flags. The data plane runs workflows, renders the UI and calls adapters. Published versions live in the configuration registry, which is the system of record, and the runtime only reads approved releases. I'd partition mainly by tenant ID, with queues and backpressure shielding external dependencies. The hardest trade-off is how far customer logic may go inside approved extensions, versus keeping it all as declarative config. For the MVP I'd keep extensions narrow, insist on versioned configs, and send every release through a tenant test harness and a staged flag rollout. My first production gate is one tenant, with a rollback I can run straight away."

sections.text: 5. Data Model, APIs, and Working CodeFour Core Records and Ownership Interviewers trust concrete state over abstractions. Tie the riskiest parts of the design to records, contracts and a little code. Say what is durable and what can change. Say what carries a version, what gets deployed, and what the system does when an identical request arrives a second time. WorkflowTemplate(id, engine_version, schema): the shared blueprint. Product and platform own it. id is the primary key. engine_version names the evaluator and renderer that can read this template. schema sets the permitted shape of fields, approvals and integrations. Lifecycle: draft → published. Once published, the artifact never changes; new behaviour needs a new template version. Retention: hold published templates for as long as the product or contract window lasts. Older tenant configs must still resolve against the precise template they were validated with. Drafts can be garbage-collected once they have sat idle for a safe period. TenantConfig(tenant_id, template_id, version, values): the overlay one customer applies on top of a template. In practice the key is (tenant_id, version). values carries only the tenant parameters that the template schema permits. Lifecycle: draft → validated → deployed or rolled_back. When validation fails, the record goes back to draft/needs_fix and keeps its version number. Retention: every published and rolled-back version stays, so audit and rollback both work. Drafts follow platform policy and are dropped once abandoned or superseded. What the values mean for the business is the tenant's call. Validating and storing them is the platform's job. AdapterDefinition(name, contract_version, permissions): the contract for talking to one downstream system, such as CRM (customer relationship management), ticketing, storage or messaging. name plus contract_version form the key. permissions lists the scopes and capabilities the adapter needs, so the platform can turn down a config that requests an adapter it has no safe way to call. Lifecycle: the platform or integrations team runs it. Contracts ship as versions and retire only when no active tenant config still relies on them. Retention: retired definitions stay around for past deployments and debugging. They are flagged inactive, so a new config cannot pick them. ConfigDeployment(tenant_id, version, state): the deployment ledger. It alone decides which of draft / validated / deployed / rolled_back / failed applies. Ops and support read this record to see which version is live at this moment. Lifecycle: each state change is appended; nothing is rewritten in place. A rollback adds a fresh deployment event that points at an earlier good version. Retention: hold the whole history for the full support and audit window. Incident reviews, customer support and change tracking all depend on it. Separate owners stop the records from tangling. Product owns the template. The customer owns the tenant config. Integrations owns the adapter contract. Ops owns the deployment record. Blur those lines and per-customer forks return. Interview pointer: If asked what tells you which version is live, answer ConfigDeployment, not TenantConfig. Its state transitions are append-only. That ledger lets support see what is running now, and it turns a rollback into a new event rather than an edit in place. Four API Contracts At interview scale, show one bounded declarative contract plus a write path that stops unsafe input before the registry ever sees it. It proves three things: the platform takes limited configuration, checks it, and publishes it as an immutable version. POST /v1/configurations/validate: takes a draft tenant config and hands back validation errors plus a normalised preview. It never publishes anything. 5. Data Model, APIs, and Working Code

Four Core Records and Ownership
  • Interviewers trust concrete state over abstractions. Tie the riskiest parts of the design to records, contracts and a little code. Say what is durable and what can change. Say what carries a version, what gets deployed, and what the system does when an identical request arrives a second time.
  • WorkflowTemplate(id, engine_version, schema): the shared blueprint. Product and platform own it.
    • id is the primary key. engine_version names the evaluator and renderer that can read this template. schema sets the permitted shape of fields, approvals and integrations.
    • Lifecycle: draft → published. Once published, the artifact never changes; new behaviour needs a new template version.
    • Retention: hold published templates for as long as the product or contract window lasts. Older tenant configs must still resolve against the precise template they were validated with. Drafts can be garbage-collected once they have sat idle for a safe period.
  • TenantConfig(tenant_id, template_id, version, values): the overlay one customer applies on top of a template.
    • In practice the key is (tenant_id, version). values carries only the tenant parameters that the template schema permits.
    • Lifecycle: draft → validated → deployed or rolled_back. When validation fails, the record goes back to draft/needs_fix and keeps its version number.
    • Retention: every published and rolled-back version stays, so audit and rollback both work. Drafts follow platform policy and are dropped once abandoned or superseded.
    • What the values mean for the business is the tenant's call. Validating and storing them is the platform's job.
  • AdapterDefinition(name, contract_version, permissions): the contract for talking to one downstream system, such as CRM (customer relationship management), ticketing, storage or messaging.
    • name plus contract_version form the key. permissions lists the scopes and capabilities the adapter needs, so the platform can turn down a config that requests an adapter it has no safe way to call.
    • Lifecycle: the platform or integrations team runs it. Contracts ship as versions and retire only when no active tenant config still relies on them.
    • Retention: retired definitions stay around for past deployments and debugging. They are flagged inactive, so a new config cannot pick them.
  • ConfigDeployment(tenant_id, version, state): the deployment ledger. It alone decides which of draft / validated / deployed / rolled_back / failed applies.
    • Ops and support read this record to see which version is live at this moment.
    • Lifecycle: each state change is appended; nothing is rewritten in place. A rollback adds a fresh deployment event that points at an earlier good version.
    • Retention: hold the whole history for the full support and audit window. Incident reviews, customer support and change tracking all depend on it.
  • Separate owners stop the records from tangling. Product owns the template. The customer owns the tenant config. Integrations owns the adapter contract. Ops owns the deployment record. Blur those lines and per-customer forks return.

Interview pointer: If asked what tells you which version is live, answer ConfigDeployment, not TenantConfig. Its state transitions are append-only. That ledger lets support see what is running now, and it turns a rollback into a new event rather than an edit in place.

    • Auth: a bearer token or session scoped to the caller's tenant. Authorisation permits validation only for tenants the caller is allowed to administer.
    • Body: template_id, version, values, and an optional idempotency_key so validation traces can be replayed. The call has no write effects, so retrying it is safe anyway.
    • Responses: 200 OK for a good preview; 400 Bad Request when the structure is wrong; 403 Forbidden for a tenant mismatch or missing rights; 422 Unprocessable Content when schema or policy rules fail.
  • POST /v1/tenants/{id}/deployments: starts a deployment for a tenant, usually from a config version that already passed validation. It returns the deployment ID and its state.
    • Auth: the caller must belong to tenant {id} or hold a delegated ops role. The server refuses any attempt to deploy into another tenant.
    • Because this call creates something, it needs an idempotency key. The same key with an identical body gives back the same result. The same key with a different body gets 422 Unprocessable Content, as the IETF Idempotency-Key draft recommends. If a retry arrives while the first request is still in progress, it gets 409 Conflict.
    • Errors: 401 Unauthorized when credentials are absent or expired; 403 Forbidden when tenant permission is missing; 404 Not Found when the named config version does not exist; 409 Conflict for a stale optimistic-concurrency token or a key that is still in flight; 422 Unprocessable Content when syntax passes but policy fails, or when a key is reused with a different payload.
  • POST /v1/adapters/{name}/test: runs an adapter mapping against a harmless test payload or a sandbox endpoint.
    • Auth: limited to integration maintainers or tenant admins.
    • Body: the adapter name, a test payload, the mapping and an optional sandbox selector. An idempotency key is accepted too, so a retry does not produce a second test run or a second audit entry.
    • Errors: 404 Not Found for an unknown adapter; 403 Forbidden when permission is lacking; 422 Unprocessable Content when the mapping cannot be applied; 502 Bad Gateway, or something like it, when the sandbox dependency fails.
  • POST /v1/deployments/{id}/rollback: records a new rollback state for that tenant. The old deployment is left untouched.
    • Auth: the caller needs tenant scope and either raised ops rights or an explicit sign-off route.
    • Body: identifies the target deployment or the earlier good version. It carries an idempotency key, because rollback writes state and may be retried after a failure.
    • On success the caller gets the new deployment record. The previous record is never overwritten.
    • Errors: 404 Not Found when no deployment has that ID; 409 Conflict when the live state has changed so much that rolling back is unsafe; 422 Unprocessable Content when the target version no longer fits the current template or adapter contract.
  • Rules shared by all four: authentication and authorisation are tenant-aware, and writes across tenants are refused. Create-style calls demand an idempotency key. A repeat with the same key and body returns the same answer. A reused key with a new body is rejected; it never becomes a quiet update.
Idempotent Deployment Creation Walkthrough
  • Worked case: an ops client calls POST /v1/tenants/acme/deployments. Its body is {configVersion: 17, templateId: "tpl-9"}; its key is deploy-2024-11-18-001.
    • The server makes deployment dep-555 and replies 201 Created with deployment_id=dep-555 and state=deployed. The write log stores the idempotency key alongside.
    • The client times out and retries with that key. No dep-556 may appear. The reply is identical and still refers to dep-555.
    • The client then retries with that key but sends configVersion: 18. The payload no longer matches what the key was first used for, so the server answers 422.
The Smallest Safe Code Path: Config Publication
  • Config publication carries the most risk. Bad structure, broken mappings or faulty versioning at this step can take production down. The sketch below is small but contains every control point a live system needs.
type JsonValue = string | number | boolean | null | JsonValue[] | { [key: string]: JsonValue };
type JsonLogic = { op: string; args?: JsonValue[] };

type WorkflowConfig = {
  version: 1;
  fields: Array<{ key: string; type: "text" | "number" | "date"; required: boolean }>;
  approvals: Array<{ when: JsonLogic; role: string; slaHours: number }>;
  integrations: Array<{ adapter: string; mapping: Record<string, string> }>;
};

type ValidationError = { path: string; code: string; message: string };

type PublishResult =
  | { ok: true; configId: string; version: number }
  | { ok: false; errors: ValidationError[] };

class ConfigValidationError extends Error {
  constructor(public errors: ValidationError[]) {
    super("Configuration validation failed");
  }
}

function isPlainObject(value: unknown): value is Record<string, unknown> {
  return typeof value === "object" && value !== null && !Array.isArray(value);
}

function validateWorkflowConfig(input: unknown): WorkflowConfig {
  const errors: ValidationError[] = [];

  if (!isPlainObject(input)) {
    throw new ConfigValidationError([{ path: "$", code: "invalid_type", message: "Expected an object" }]);
  }

  if (input.version !== 1) {
    errors.push({ path: "version", code: "unsupported_version", message: "Only version 1 is supported" });
  }

  if (!Array.isArray(input.fields) || input.fields.length === 0) {
    errors.push({ path: "fields", code: "required", message: "At least one field is required" });
  }

  if (!Array.isArray(input.approvals)) {
    errors.push({ path: "approvals", code: "invalid_type", message: "Approvals must be an array" });
  }

  if (!Array.isArray(input.integrations)) {
    errors.push({ path: "integrations", code: "invalid_type", message: "Integrations must be an array" });
  }

  if (errors.length > 0) {
    throw new ConfigValidationError(errors);
  }

  return input as WorkflowConfig;
}

function validatePolicy(config: WorkflowConfig): void {
  const seenRoles = new Set<string>();
  for (const approval of config.approvals) {
    if (!approval.role || approval.slaHours <= 0) {
      throw new ConfigValidationError([
        { path: "approvals", code: "invalid_approval", message: "Each approval must have a role and positive SLA" },
      ]);
    }
    if (seenRoles.has(approval.role)) {
      throw new ConfigValidationError([
        { path: "approvals", code: "duplicate_role", message: `Duplicate approval role: ${approval.role}` },
      ]);
    }
    seenRoles.add(approval.role);
  }
}

function validateAdapterMappings(config: WorkflowConfig, allowedAdapters: Set<string>): void {
  for (const integration of config.integrations) {
    if (!allowedAdapters.has(integration.adapter)) {
      throw new ConfigValidationError([
        { path: "integrations", code: "unknown_adapter", message: `Unknown adapter: ${integration.adapter}` },
      ]);
    }
    for (const [from, to] of Object.entries(integration.mapping)) {
      if (!from || !to) {
        throw new ConfigValidationError([
          { path: `integrations.${integration.adapter}.mapping`, code: "invalid_mapping", message: "Mappings must not contain empty keys" },
        ]);
      }
    }
  }
}

class Registry {
  private store = new Map<string, { version: number; config: WorkflowConfig; hash: string }>();

  putImmutable(configId: string, config: WorkflowConfig): { version: number } {
    const existing = this.store.get(configId);
    const nextVersion = existing ? existing.version + 1 : 1;
    const hash = JSON.stringify(config);
    this.store.set(configId, { version: nextVersion, config, hash });
    return { version: nextVersion };
  }
}

function publish(configId: string, raw: unknown, allowedAdapters: Set<string>, registry: Registry): PublishResult {
  try {
    const config = validateWorkflowConfig(raw);
    validatePolicy(config);
    validateAdapterMappings(config, allowedAdapters);
    const result = registry.putImmutable(configId, config);
    return { ok: true, configId, version: result.version };
  } catch (error) {
    if (error instanceof ConfigValidationError) {
      return { ok: false, errors: error.errors };
    }
    return {
      ok: false,
      errors: [{ path: "$", code: "internal_error", message: "Unexpected failure during publish" }],
    };
  }
}
  • What each part teaches:
    • WorkflowConfig limits the shape to a declarative contract with a version.
    • JsonValue/JsonLogic state approval conditions openly and leave no route for arbitrary code.
    • ValidationError hands the API a fixed set of error terms.
    • validateWorkflowConfig validates types at the boundary. Malformed payloads stop there, before any business logic runs.
    • validatePolicy keeps authorisation and workflow rules apart from structural checks.
    • validateAdapterMappings compares the integration surface with an allowlist instead of trusting whoever wrote the config.
    • Registry.putImmutable stores each write as a new version; nothing is overwritten.
    • publish runs the checks in the one order that holds up: parse → validate → authorise-by-policy → persist.

Interview pointer: Commit the sequence to memory and reuse it elsewhere: parse → validate → authorise-by-policy → persist. Expect the follow-up "why that order?" Cheap structural checks come first and fail fast, so the costly policy and adapter checks only run on sound input. Nothing is written until every earlier step passes, so the path fails closed.

What the Whiteboard Version Omits on Purpose
  • A production service would also need:
    • Optimistic concurrency: each write should state the template or config version it expects, so two operators cannot race and silently overwrite each other. If the version travels in the body, a mismatch returns 409 Conflict. If it travels in an If-Match header, HTTP calls for 412 Precondition Failed.
    • Idempotency: retrying after a timeout must never yield a second deployment or a second version.
    • Bounded, safe retries: retry only failure types that are safe to repeat. Never replay a rejected validation or authorisation; it is not transient.
    • Observability: each validation, deployment, adapter test and rollback should carry the request ID, the tenant ID, the idempotency key and the config version. Support can then rebuild exactly what happened without combing through application logs.
Contract and Failure-Injection Tests
  • A strong answer brings two tests. One pins the contract; the other injects a failure.
import { describe, it, expect } from "vitest";

describe("publish", () => {
  it("rejects duplicate approval roles and returns a structured validation error", () => {
    const registry = new Registry();
    const result = publish(
      "cfg-1",
      {
        version: 1,
        fields: [{ key: "requester", type: "text", required: true }],
        approvals: [
          { when: { op: "always" }, role: "manager", slaHours: 24 },
          { when: { op: "always" }, role: "manager", slaHours: 24 },
        ],
        integrations: [],
      },
      new Set(["crm"]),
      registry,
    );

    expect(result.ok).toBe(false);
    if (!result.ok) {
      expect(result.errors[0].code).toBe("duplicate_role");
    }
  });

  it("survives an adapter allowlist miss without publishing state", () => {
    const registry = new Registry();
    const result = publish(
      "cfg-2",
      {
        version: 1,
        fields: [{ key: "requester", type: "text", required: true }],
        approvals: [{ when: { op: "always" }, role: "manager", slaHours: 24 }],
        integrations: [{ adapter: "unknown", mapping: { a: "b" } }],
      },
      new Set(["crm"]),
      registry,
    );

    expect(result.ok).toBe(false);
  });
});

  • The failure-injection test feeds in an unsafe adapter definition and confirms that publishing fails closed.
  • A real service would add more: tests for duplicate idempotency keys, tests for deployment rollback, and a concurrency test proving that stale versions are refused.

sections.text: 6. Security, Reliability, and Failure HandlingThe Red-Team Question The security and operations review decides whether this platform ships or stays a good demo. Assume the hardest realistic request: deep workflow control for customers, a core that stays stable anyway, secrets kept per tenant, and one customer's broken config that never becomes everyone's outage. A sharp reviewer asks: "A config goes live and its approvals loop forever. Then what?" The test is whether the platform limits the damage, keeps the evidence and keeps serving every other tenant. Before activation, the config pipeline turns away any cycle it can see. Some loops only appear after publish, through hidden state or a race. When that happens, the engine stops that workflow version and marks the bad revision inactive. Customers can still use the version that last worked. For audit and replay, the system logs who published, when, for which tenant, plus a snapshot of the rule graph. Loops will happen; make each one dull, bounded and traced to a named change. Four Security Controls Disallow arbitrary code by default. Customers shape workflows through declarations: fields, validation rules, routing, approvals and adapter bindings. Custom code is a last resort; if ever allowed, it runs in a tightly limited sandbox or behind a separate, approval-gated extension path. Scope adapters and secrets per tenant. Compartmentalise every integration so no tenant sees a neighbour's credentials, tokens or request bodies. Apply least privilege in two places: the runtime that carries out actions, and the control plane that publishes config. A support engineer allowed to read a tenant's config does not, by that fact, get to call that tenant's external systems. Validate rules for denial-of-service risk. Rich validation can turn into a way to exhaust resources. Deeply nested conditions, unbounded regexes, huge lookup tables and recursive approval paths can each burn CPU or memory without limit. So the publish path checks shape, depth and size against fixed caps, and runs cycle detection, before any config goes live. Audit configuration publishers and versions. Each change leaves a lasting record: the publisher, the diff, the review or approval gate it passed, and the version it replaced. With it, operations can find the revision that broke things, and security can confirm the change was authorised. In the interview, pair each control with the failure it stops: running code, leaking secrets, abusing resources and losing track of who changed what. Failure-Policy Decision Table Event Default behaviour Why Checks at publish cannot show the workflow is safe to switch on Fail closed Blocking a doubtful publish costs less than running an unsafe revision for a tenant An external adapter hits its timeout mid-run Bounded retries, then a queue or the dead-letter path A brief outage should not fail the customer's work on the spot The approval graph contains a cycle, or starts looping while running Fail closed for that workflow version The loop will do the same harm every time; letting it run only adds more An integration further down is offline, yet the task is not urgent Degrade or queue Hold the work rather than lose it, as long as the SLA tolerates the wait The customer's action cannot be undone, for example a side effect in another system When in doubt, hand it to a human When the system has no safe way to undo, it must not guess Someone asks for custom code that looks suspicious Deny by default Execution rights need a clear trust boundary before the platform hands them out Lead with this table. It shows you designed failure handling up front. Blast-Radius Containment Levels Tenant blast radius: a broken config from one customer must leave every other customer's workflow state, secrets and run queue untouched. Region blast radius: in a multi-region setup, keep a faulty deploy or a failing dependency inside the smallest region slice you can. Workflow blast radius: freeze only the workflow definition or version at fault. The rest of the tenant keeps running, unless its control plane itself is compromised. 6. Security, Reliability, and Failure Handling

The Red-Team Question
  • The security and operations review decides whether this platform ships or stays a good demo. Assume the hardest realistic request: deep workflow control for customers, a core that stays stable anyway, secrets kept per tenant, and one customer's broken config that never becomes everyone's outage.
  • A sharp reviewer asks: "A config goes live and its approvals loop forever. Then what?" The test is whether the platform limits the damage, keeps the evidence and keeps serving every other tenant.
  • Before activation, the config pipeline turns away any cycle it can see. Some loops only appear after publish, through hidden state or a race. When that happens, the engine stops that workflow version and marks the bad revision inactive. Customers can still use the version that last worked. For audit and replay, the system logs who published, when, for which tenant, plus a snapshot of the rule graph. Loops will happen; make each one dull, bounded and traced to a named change.
Four Security Controls
  • Disallow arbitrary code by default. Customers shape workflows through declarations: fields, validation rules, routing, approvals and adapter bindings. Custom code is a last resort; if ever allowed, it runs in a tightly limited sandbox or behind a separate, approval-gated extension path.
  • Scope adapters and secrets per tenant. Compartmentalise every integration so no tenant sees a neighbour's credentials, tokens or request bodies. Apply least privilege in two places: the runtime that carries out actions, and the control plane that publishes config. A support engineer allowed to read a tenant's config does not, by that fact, get to call that tenant's external systems.
  • Validate rules for denial-of-service risk. Rich validation can turn into a way to exhaust resources. Deeply nested conditions, unbounded regexes, huge lookup tables and recursive approval paths can each burn CPU or memory without limit. So the publish path checks shape, depth and size against fixed caps, and runs cycle detection, before any config goes live.
  • Audit configuration publishers and versions. Each change leaves a lasting record: the publisher, the diff, the review or approval gate it passed, and the version it replaced. With it, operations can find the revision that broke things, and security can confirm the change was authorised.
  • In the interview, pair each control with the failure it stops: running code, leaking secrets, abusing resources and losing track of who changed what.
Failure-Policy Decision Table
Event Default behaviour Why
Checks at publish cannot show the workflow is safe to switch on Fail closed Blocking a doubtful publish costs less than running an unsafe revision for a tenant
An external adapter hits its timeout mid-run Bounded retries, then a queue or the dead-letter path A brief outage should not fail the customer's work on the spot
The approval graph contains a cycle, or starts looping while running Fail closed for that workflow version The loop will do the same harm every time; letting it run only adds more
An integration further down is offline, yet the task is not urgent Degrade or queue Hold the work rather than lose it, as long as the SLA tolerates the wait
The customer's action cannot be undone, for example a side effect in another system When in doubt, hand it to a human When the system has no safe way to undo, it must not guess
Someone asks for custom code that looks suspicious Deny by default Execution rights need a clear trust boundary before the platform hands them out

export type WorkflowConfig = {
  tenantId: string;
  version: number;
  fields: Array<{ key: string; type: string; required?: boolean }>;
  approvals: Array<{ when: Record<string, unknown>; role: string; slaHours?: number }>;
  integrations: Array<{ adapter: string; mapping: Record<string, string> }>;
};

export type AdapterRegistry = {
  has(adapterName: string): boolean;
};

export type PublishResult =
  | { ok: true; activatedVersion: number }
  | { ok: false; error: string };

const ALLOWED_FIELD_TYPES = new Set(["text", "number", "date", "boolean", "email"]);
const MAX_FIELDS = 50;
const MAX_APPROVALS = 10;
const MAX_INTEGRATIONS = 20;

function isPlainObject(value: unknown): value is Record<string, unknown> {
  return typeof value === "object" && value !== null && !Array.isArray(value);
}

function validateConfig(config: WorkflowConfig, registry: AdapterRegistry): string | null {
  if (!config.tenantId || typeof config.tenantId !== "string") return "invalid tenantId";
  if (!Number.isInteger(config.version) || config.version < 1) return "invalid version";
  if (!Array.isArray(config.fields) || config.fields.length > MAX_FIELDS) return "invalid fields";
  if (!Array.isArray(config.approvals) || config.approvals.length > MAX_APPROVALS) return "invalid approvals";
  if (!Array.isArray(config.integrations) || config.integrations.length > MAX_INTEGRATIONS) return "invalid integrations";

  const seenFields = new Set<string>();
  for (const field of config.fields) {
    if (!field || typeof field.key !== "string" || !field.key.trim()) return "invalid field key";
    if (seenFields.has(field.key)) return "duplicate field key";
    seenFields.add(field.key);
    if (!ALLOWED_FIELD_TYPES.has(field.type)) return `unsupported field type: ${field.type}`;
  }

  for (const approval of config.approvals) {
    if (!approval || typeof approval.role !== "string" || !approval.role.trim()) return "invalid approval role";
    if (!isPlainObject(approval.when)) return "invalid approval condition";
    if (approval.slaHours !== undefined && (!Number.isInteger(approval.slaHours) || approval.slaHours < 1 || approval.slaHours > 168)) {
      return "invalid approval slaHours";
    }
  }

  for (const integration of config.integrations) {
    if (!integration || typeof integration.adapter !== "string" || !integration.adapter.trim()) return "invalid adapter name";
    if (!registry.has(integration.adapter)) return `unknown adapter: ${integration.adapter}`;
    if (!isPlainObject(integration.mapping)) return "invalid adapter mapping";
  }

  return null;
}

export function publish(config: WorkflowConfig, registry: AdapterRegistry): PublishResult {
  const error = validateConfig(config, registry);
  if (error) {
    return { ok: false, error };
  }

  return { ok: true, activatedVersion: config.version };
}

export function configWithAdapter(adapterName: string): WorkflowConfig {
  return {
    tenantId: "tenant-acme",
    version: 1,
    fields: [{ key: "requester", type: "text", required: true }],
    approvals: [{ when: { op: "always" }, role: "manager", slaHours: 24 }],
    integrations: [{ adapter: adapterName, mapping: { a: "b" } }],
  };
}

// Example failure test.
describe("publish", () => {
  it("rejects an unknown adapter", () => {
    const registry: AdapterRegistry = { has: (adapterName: string) => adapterName === "crm" };

    expect(() => {
      const result = publish(configWithAdapter("arbitrary-shell"), registry);
      if (result.ok) throw new Error("expected publish to fail");
      throw new Error(result.error);
    }).toThrow(/unknown adapter/);
  });

  it("accepts a known adapter", () => {
    const registry: AdapterRegistry = { has: (adapterName: string) => adapterName === "crm" };
    const result = publish(configWithAdapter("crm"), registry);
    expect(result.ok).toBe(true);
  });
});
  • The test makes the invariant plain without claiming the code is finished. If a config names an adapter the platform has never heard of, the tenant cannot activate it, and publish fails closed long before runtime.
What to Say in the Interview
  • Show your judgement out loud. Arbitrary code is off unless explicitly allowed. Each tenant's secrets and adapters live in their own compartment. Risky rules are checked before they go live. Every publish leaves an audit trail. Each external dependency and each irreversible action has a named failure policy. Then link all of this to supportability: with evidence in hand, the platform can degrade, queue or block, and it never has to guess.
  • Hiring teams want someone who owns safe rollout, support and incident response beyond the happy path, and who guards the product core while customers still feel their workflows bend to fit them.
  • Give every external dependency and every irreversible action an explicit policy for failure and recovery. State that policy at four levels (tenant, region, workflow and dependency), and back it with a publish-time invariant so unsafe config never reaches production.

sections.text: 7. Delivery Plan, Observability, and Business ImpactRollout as a Series of Proofs When the prototype works, the customer stops asking whether the platform can do the job. They start asking whether they can trust it in production, with their own data, their own approval chains and their own support staff. Now the FDE (Forward Deployed Engineer) stops building demos and turns the architecture into staged delivery, with a measurable gate at every stage. Do not plan one big go-live. Plan a sequence of proofs: Start with a workflow that several customers already share. Pick its least contested form: a single approval path, a single integration, a single field set and a single brand surface. Go deep: show that a real customer need fits the platform with no fork. Next, bring on one willing customer who copes with loose ends and gives feedback quickly. Name an owner on your side, keep a single production gate, and know the rollback path before the first publish. Release as a canary first, to a thin slice of traffic or to one low-risk group of tenants. Keep the first launch small enough that support can trace each event, each rejected config and each request sent to a downstream system. Widen the configuration surface only when evidence keeps showing three things: the current surface meets real demand, it cuts duplicated work, and it adds no incident risk. Without that rule, the platform turns into a growing pile of tenant-specific debt. The Four-Phase Rollout Plan Extract one recurring workflow. Owner: a product engineer, with the FDE in support. Exit criteria: shared primitives can express the workflow, so no one-off fork is needed. Go/no-go gate: the team judges the pattern settled enough to build into the platform. Onboard a willing customer. Owner: the FDE together with the customer admin. Exit criteria: the customer configures the workflow, finishes a pilot run and raises issues through the support channel. Go/no-go gate: the customer signs up to the support model and the rollback procedure. Measure delivery time and defects. Owner: the platform lead for telemetry, and the support lead for classifying incidents. Exit criteria: starting figures exist for how fast tenants launch, how many defects appear and how often validation fails, all captured before any scope is added. Go/no-go gate: the data shows configuration is cutting custom work, not hiding rework somewhere else. Expand configuration only after repeated evidence. Owner: product and platform, deciding together. Exit criteria: a second and a third customer reuse the same mechanism, and the effort is predictable. Go/no-go gate: a new config type is approved only if it reduces forks or support load without adding upgrade risk. Interview pointer: Interviewers tend to push on the gates between phases, so know all four by heart. The pattern is stable. The customer accepts the support and rollback model. The evidence shows config cuts custom work. Customers two and three reuse it with no fresh build. These gates stop a rollout from becoming "we shipped because the demo went well." The Six-Metric Scorecard Time to launch customer: the time from an approved request to a tenant's first successful production workflow. Data from: release tracking and ticket timestamps. Owner: delivery lead. Alert when: lead time creeps up across several customers, a sign of brittle config, slow approvals or manual steps. Percentage handled by configuration: of all customer-specific changes, the share delivered as config rather than code. Data from: tags on releases and change requests. Owner: product or platform lead. Alert when: the share stops rising, which usually means the team is quietly going back to forks. Config validation failure rate: failed publishes divided by all publish attempts. Data from: config service logs. Owner: platform engineering. Alert when: the rate climbs, which points to a confusing UX, a weak schema or unsafe requests. Fork count: how many customer-specific code branches, conditionals or exceptions exist that cannot be removed. Data from: architecture reviews and repository analysis. Owner: engineering manager. Alert when: the count grows, since every fork erodes the stable core. Upgrade time: the effort to move one customer or tenant onto a new platform version. Data from: release records and migration tickets. Owner: release manager. Alert when: an upgrade needs one-off scripts or a long freeze window. Tenant incident rate: a rolling count of each tenant's incidents, kept separate from outages that hit the whole platform. Data from: the incident management system. Owner: support and SRE (site reliability engineering) together. Alert when: incidents bunch around one config type or one adapter. Four Layers of Metrics Technical health: how often publishes succeed, validation failures, how often rollbacks happen, latency and incident rate. Model/config quality: do the workflow primitives fit how customers really work? The usual clue is how often customers ask for exceptions. Adoption: customer count on the configured workflow, how frequently each one returns, and the share of each customer's process it now handles. Business outcome: faster launches, less custom engineering, fewer support escalations and quicker growth into new tenants. Keep the layers apart in an interview. A platform can pass every technical check and still fail commercially because nobody adopts it. It can also be widely adopted and still fail in operation because support cannot keep it stable. Dashboard in the Language of the User Lead with the customer's story, then drill down into the machinery. A headline might read, with illustrative numbers: "Onboarding for this customer took under two days. It needed zero manual config edits and one validation retry, and there was no incident after launch." Under that headline sit the internal signals, broken out by tenant: rollout status, publish latency, adapter errors, blocked approval loops and failed schema validations. Use this to answer "what do we watch after launch?". CPU, logs and queue depth are not enough. The dashboard should link what the customer sees as success to the failure modes inside the system. Ownership Before Launch Product owner: picks the first repeated workflow to turn into a platformised path. Platform owner: looks after the shared core, the config schema and the publish service. FDE: turns the customer's workflow into supported configuration, checks the assumptions and runs the rollout. Support lead: handles customer communication, triage and escalation during the pilot. SRE / operations lead: owns monitoring, rollback execution and release health. Customer admin / champion: tests the workflow in their own environment and signs off that it is ready. Go/No-Go and Rollback Triggers Go/no-go gate: a config may publish only when four things hold. Validation passes. The adapters it depends on are healthy. The team has rehearsed the rollback plan. The customer champion agrees that their business process and the configured workflow still line up. Rollback trigger: roll back on any one of these. Validation keeps failing. Integrations throw errors nobody predicted. Incidents climb among the earliest group of tenants. A new config pattern starts to make approvals unstable. For a stateful workflow, write the migration plan and the rollback plan separately. Moving state is a different job from reverting code. Ship a launch package of four documents: a short guide for admins, a runbook for support, a rollback checklist and a change log. The change log lists which parts customers may configure, which stay fixed, and which go to engineering for review. Config vs. Adapter vs. Shared Service vs. Core Configuration: fields, routing choices, branding, approver lists and threshold values that differ per customer. Adapter: integrations that vary by customer behind one common interface, such as CRM (customer relationship management), ticketing, email, identity and document systems. Shared service: capabilities every tenant reuses under one uniform policy, such as validation, audit logging, workflow execution and publish orchestration. Core product: the building blocks the business model rests on. They stay put, and no new tenant gets to reopen them. When someone asks for "just one exception", test it against these four homes. Does it change the core product? Does it belong in an adapter? Can it be modelled as config? Asking this keeps the platform from sliding into per-customer branches that nobody can maintain. The Risk Register Risk Owner Mitigation Trigger Infinite approval loop Platform engineer Detect cycles and validate at publish time The same approval state is entered again and again Adapter mismatch Integration engineer Contract tests plus explicit adapter versions Calls fail after a publish, or the schema drifts Customer confusion during rollout FDE Training, playbooks and guided setup Support volume is high, or validation errors keep repeating Unsupported fork pressure Product manager Clear grounds for refusing bespoke code, plus a review board for exceptions A request cannot be expressed in configuration Treat this register as part of running the platform, not an appendix. Forward-deployed teams want people who carry work past the prototype until customers adopt it, then distil what customers said into a pattern the product can reuse. Call the platform finished once three things are true: customers rely on it, the workflow keeps improving, and operations can run it with no heroics.

    • Widen the configuration surface only when evidence keeps showing three things: the current surface meets real demand, it cuts duplicated work, and it adds no incident risk. Without that rule, the platform turns into a growing pile of tenant-specific debt.
The Four-Phase Rollout Plan
  1. Extract one recurring workflow.
    • Owner: a product engineer, with the FDE in support.
    • Exit criteria: shared primitives can express the workflow, so no one-off fork is needed.
    • Go/no-go gate: the team judges the pattern settled enough to build into the platform.
  2. Onboard a willing customer.
    • Owner: the FDE together with the customer admin.
    • Exit criteria: the customer configures the workflow, finishes a pilot run and raises issues through the support channel.
    • Go/no-go gate: the customer signs up to the support model and the rollback procedure.
  3. Measure delivery time and defects.
    • Owner: the platform lead for telemetry, and the support lead for classifying incidents.
    • Exit criteria: starting figures exist for how fast tenants launch, how many defects appear and how often validation fails, all captured before any scope is added.
    • Go/no-go gate: the data shows configuration is cutting custom work, not hiding rework somewhere else.
  4. Expand configuration only after repeated evidence.
    • Owner: product and platform, deciding together.
    • Exit criteria: a second and a third customer reuse the same mechanism, and the effort is predictable.
    • Go/no-go gate: a new config type is approved only if it reduces forks or support load without adding upgrade risk.

Interview pointer: Interviewers tend to push on the gates between phases, so know all four by heart. The pattern is stable. The customer accepts the support and rollback model. The evidence shows config cuts custom work. Customers two and three reuse it with no fresh build. These gates stop a rollout from becoming "we shipped because the demo went well."

The Six-Metric Scorecard
  • Time to launch customer: the time from an approved request to a tenant's first successful production workflow. Data from: release tracking and ticket timestamps. Owner: delivery lead. Alert when: lead time creeps up across several customers, a sign of brittle config, slow approvals or manual steps.
  • Percentage handled by configuration: of all customer-specific changes, the share delivered as config rather than code. Data from: tags on releases and change requests. Owner: product or platform lead. Alert when: the share stops rising, which usually means the team is quietly going back to forks.
  • Config validation failure rate: failed publishes divided by all publish attempts. Data from: config service logs. Owner: platform engineering. Alert when: the rate climbs, which points to a confusing UX, a weak schema or unsafe requests.
  • Fork count: how many customer-specific code branches, conditionals or exceptions exist that cannot be removed. Data from: architecture reviews and repository analysis. Owner: engineering manager. Alert when: the count grows, since every fork erodes the stable core.
  • Upgrade time: the effort to move one customer or tenant onto a new platform version. Data from: release records and migration tickets. Owner: release manager. Alert when: an upgrade needs one-off scripts or a long freeze window.
  • Tenant incident rate: a rolling count of each tenant's incidents, kept separate from outages that hit the whole platform. Data from: the incident management system. Owner: support and SRE (site reliability engineering) together. Alert when: incidents bunch around one config type or one adapter.
Four Layers of Metrics
  • Technical health: how often publishes succeed, validation failures, how often rollbacks happen, latency and incident rate.
  • Model/config quality: do the workflow primitives fit how customers really work? The usual clue is how often customers ask for exceptions.
  • Adoption: customer count on the configured workflow, how frequently each one returns, and the share of each customer's process it now handles.
  • Business outcome: faster launches, less custom engineering, fewer support escalations and quicker growth into new tenants.
  • Keep the layers apart in an interview. A platform can pass every technical check and still fail commercially because nobody adopts it. It can also be widely adopted and still fail in operation because support cannot keep it stable.
Dashboard in the Language of the User
  • Lead with the customer's story, then drill down into the machinery. A headline might read, with illustrative numbers: "Onboarding for this customer took under two days. It needed zero manual config edits and one validation retry, and there was no incident after launch."
  • Under that headline sit the internal signals, broken out by tenant: rollout status, publish latency, adapter errors, blocked approval loops and failed schema validations.
  • Use this to answer "what do we watch after launch?". CPU, logs and queue depth are not enough. The dashboard should link what the customer sees as success to the failure modes inside the system.
Ownership Before Launch
  • Product owner: picks the first repeated workflow to turn into a platformised path.
  • Platform owner: looks after the shared core, the config schema and the publish service.
  • FDE: turns the customer's workflow into supported configuration, checks the assumptions and runs the rollout.
  • Support lead: handles customer communication, triage and escalation during the pilot.
  • SRE / operations lead: owns monitoring, rollback execution and release health.
  • Customer admin / champion: tests the workflow in their own environment and signs off that it is ready.
Go/No-Go and Rollback Triggers
  • Go/no-go gate: a config may publish only when four things hold. Validation passes. The adapters it depends on are healthy. The team has rehearsed the rollback plan. The customer champion agrees that their business process and the configured workflow still line up.
  • Rollback trigger: roll back on any one of these. Validation keeps failing. Integrations throw errors nobody predicted. Incidents climb among the earliest group of tenants. A new config pattern starts to make approvals unstable.
  • For a stateful workflow, write the migration plan and the rollback plan separately. Moving state is a different job from reverting code.
  • Ship a launch package of four documents: a short guide for admins, a runbook for support, a rollback checklist and a change log. The change log lists which parts customers may configure, which stay fixed, and which go to engineering for review.
Config vs. Adapter vs. Shared Service vs. Core
  • Configuration: fields, routing choices, branding, approver lists and threshold values that differ per customer.
  • Adapter: integrations that vary by customer behind one common interface, such as CRM (customer relationship management), ticketing, email, identity and document systems.
  • Shared service: capabilities every tenant reuses under one uniform policy, such as validation, audit logging, workflow execution and publish orchestration.
  • Core product: the building blocks the business model rests on. They stay put, and no new tenant gets to reopen them.
  • When someone asks for "just one exception", test it against these four homes. Does it change the core product? Does it belong in an adapter? Can it be modelled as config? Asking this keeps the platform from sliding into per-customer branches that nobody can maintain.
The Risk Register
Risk Owner Mitigation Trigger
Infinite approval loop Platform engineer Detect cycles and validate at publish time The same approval state is entered again and again
Adapter mismatch Integration engineer Contract tests plus explicit adapter versions Calls fail after a publish, or the schema drifts
Customer confusion during rollout FDE Training, playbooks and guided setup Support volume is high, or validation errors keep repeating
Unsupported fork pressure Product manager Clear grounds for refusing bespoke code, plus a review board for exceptions A request cannot be expressed in configuration
  • Treat this register as part of running the platform, not an appendix.
  • Forward-deployed teams want people who carry work past the prototype until customers adopt it, then distil what customers said into a pattern the product can reuse. Call the platform finished once three things are true: customers rely on it, the workflow keeps improving, and operations can run it with no heroics.

glossary.definition: Forward Deployed Engineer: An engineer who sits with the customer, figures out the real problem, and ships a working system in their environment.
site reliability engineering: The team and practice that keeps production running: on-call, SLOs, incident response.
customer relationship management: The sales and customer system of record — Salesforce is the usual example.

Which parts belong in the product core? Which parts can each tenant change safely through configuration? And which extensions must run in strict isolation? I'd lean towards a small, stable core, with tenant differences held in configuration that is versioned and tested. I'd depart from that only for a need that is genuinely one of a kind, or too dangerous to make generic." Those sentences carry the outcome, show architectural judgement and invite pushback. If the interviewer shifts the ground, for example with a regulated sign-off step or a proprietary connector, rework the plan instead of defending your first guess. The 50-Minute Pacing Plan Spend minutes by risk, not by the size of the boxes. A strong candidate lingers on the part whose failure would cost the business most. Outcome and discovery, minutes 0–9. Minute 0: anchor on the outcome. Minute 1: the main thing the customer gets. Minute 2: which piece of the workflow moves fastest. Minute 3: surface the hidden constraint. Minute 4: what must never shift. Minute 5: the fixed requirements, namely identity, workflow semantics, auditability, rollback and support boundaries. Minutes 6 to 8: assumptions, first on tenant numbers and change rate, next on who drafts and signs off config, last on failure tolerance and incident handling. Minute 9: offer the interviewer a chance to redirect. Success and scale, minutes 10–14. Minute 10: success for the customer and for the team running the platform. Minute 11: what that implies for SLOs (service level objectives) and for support. Minute 12: what "safe customisation" should mean here. Minute 13: a rough load shape: tenants, workflows, connectors, admin edits. Minute 14: call every figure illustrative. Architecture, minutes 15–24. Minute 15: the overall design. Then one component a minute: authoring tools and their guardrails (16), validation and the gates before publish (17), immutable versions and how they roll out (18), the engine that runs workflows (19), connectors and where integrations stop (20), audit logs and observability (21), per-tenant identity and authorisation (22), reads and writes of workflow state (23). Minute 24: contrast the control path with the data path. Config lifecycle, minutes 25–29. Who may change a tenant's settings (25). Who checks the change (26). How it moves between environments (27). How you undo it (28). How support pins a version and reproduces a reported problem (29). Happy path, failure path, loop drill, minutes 30–38. Trace a good change from edit to publish (30), from publish to a running workflow (31), and from that run to its audit entry (32). Then break it: a config that fails validation (33), permissions that have drifted (34), a connector that stops responding (35), a bad publish that needs reverting (36). Minute 37 is the drill where approvals circle forever. Minute 38 shows how cycle detection and checks at publish time stop that loop before production. Trade-offs and follow-ups, minutes 39–46. Config against code (39). A generic engine against a domain product (40). Plugin freedom against security (41). Compatibility against simplicity (42). Then follow-ups: what belongs in the core (43), how config versions work (44), when a single-customer fork is justified (45), and how to isolate extensions (46). Close, minutes 47–49. Recap delivery, rollout gates, observability and support runbooks (47). Give the 90-second summary for executives (48). State the first gate for production rollout, then invite questions (49). Four Trade-Off Pairs Configuration versus code. When tenants vary only in fields, labels, approvals, routing or their choice of connector, use configuration. Such differences stay visible, carry version numbers and remain easy to support. Reach for code once the variation changes what the workflow means, adds a new invariant, or would twist the config language into a programming language nobody can read. The weak line is "make everything configurable". A better one: "Put the common variations in declarative config. When a rule becomes bespoke business behaviour, promote it to reviewed, isolated code." Generic engine versus domain product. One generic engine can host many tenants. Make it model every business process and it becomes too abstract. A domain product does less but is simpler to use and cheaper to support. Combine them: a stable core built from workflow primitives the company knows it can support repeatedly, with a constrained domain model on top. Aim at the workflow family the business intends to own, not at endless extensibility. Plugin flexibility versus security. Plugins let teams wire in unusual customer systems without touching the core, so customers go live faster. The price is a larger attack surface. Contain it: run extensions in a sandbox, give them minimal permissions, fix their interfaces, and manage every plugin as a reviewed, versioned and observable artifact. Once a plugin can read lots of data or run any code it likes, it is no longer simple; treat it as a trusted service boundary. Backward compatibility versus simplification. Compatibility shields existing tenants and keeps running workflows intact. Simplification keeps the platform easy to grasp and maintain. A good candidate values both and proposes a clear deprecation policy: schemas with versions, windows for migration, tests for compatibility, and a short list of generations still supported. Promising to "support everything forever" is the weak answer; it turns support work into archaeology. Expected Follow-Up Questions What becomes core product? Put in versioned configuration: per-customer labels and field definitions, the routing of approvals, and connector parameters. If something would change how workflows execute, demand custom storage behaviour, or make rollback unsafe, keep it out of the core. Promote it only after several customers have shown they can reuse it. How do you version configurations? A published version is frozen. Diffs between versions are easy for a person to read. Saving runs the schema check; publishing runs the compatibility check. Each config lives as a declarative document recording its tenant scope, version number, who wrote it and its rollout status. Production workflows only ever run against a pinned version, never a loose draft. Versions serve audit, support and reproducing customer incidents, not only rollback. When is a one-off fork acceptable? All three conditions must hold. Nobody else could reuse the requirement. The business value outweighs the support cost. You can fence the divergence off so it never seeps into the core. Keep it rare. When it handles customer data, document and audit exactly what it may read or write. Weak: "A flexible plugin system will cover it." → Repair: name the trust boundaries, the permissions and the review gates. Weak: "If we need a fork, we can add one later." → Repair: count what forks add to support, testing and every upgrade. Weak: "Backward compatibility is always a good thing." → Repair: explain how old versions retire and how big the compatibility budget is.
