Architecture Draws boxes with no data, control or trust boundaries. Covers the main components but skips one or two flows. Walks control flow and data flow end to end, including how configuration is checked, given a version and run. Depth Stays too shallow, or digs into internals that do not matter. Balances high-level points and detail fairly well. Goes deep where failure costs most and stays brief elsewhere. Security Bolts security on at the end. Mentions basic auth and sandboxing. Builds least privilege, audit, rollback and extension boundaries into the design from day one. Delivery Leaves out rollout and support. Gestures at a phased launch. Describes a staged rollout, observability, gating on config and how to recover. Communication Hard to follow, with no closing summary. Mostly clear, but the structure is loose. Leads with the outcome, flags assumptions, makes trade-offs explicit and ends on a tight executive summary. Interview Rehearsal Checklist Before any mock or real interview, check that you can do these five things with no notes: Say the customer outcome in a single sentence. Name the hidden constraint and the assumption that carries the most risk. Explain what goes in core product and what goes in configuration. Hold your ground on one trade-off under pressure. Finish with a short summary and the first rollout gate. 90-Second Architecture Summary "We keep the workflow core small and stable. Tenant differences go into versioned configuration: fields, approvals, branding and connector settings. Customers edit their config through guarded admin tools. Every config is validated and stored as an immutable version. It publishes only if it passes the schema, policy and cycle checks. At runtime, the engine loads whichever version is live, moves each workflow from state to state and writes audit events. So support can replay what any tenant saw. Extensions plug in only through a controlled boundary. Each gets explicit contracts and minimal privilege. The main trade-off is configuration against code. I'll reuse whatever I can. But I won't push custom business semantics into config if that weakens security or makes the system hard to maintain. My first production gate is one tenant cohort. Rollback, audit and the adapter contract tests must be proven in staging before we go wider." Practice Plan Solo exercise: take a blank page and talk through the 50-minute plan out loud. Then compress it to 2 minutes and to 90 seconds. Pair mock: get a partner to cut in with a hard question, for example "What becomes core product?" or "When is a one-off fork acceptable?". Practise replying calmly, without sounding defensive. Implementation exercise: design a validator for versioned configuration. It must reject cycles in approval routing and insist on safe publish-time checks before any workflow goes live. Equation guidance: this section adds no new equation, and numbers stay in prose. The capacity maths lives in the scale section in part 2, so this walkthrough stays on trade-offs. sections.text: Coverage NotesWe reviewed this guide once against our 20-point checklist for design case studies. Almost every point was met on that first pass, so the notes below record the result and flag where the guide is thin. Phase 1: Problem Framing & Discovery Item 1 (turning the feature request into a business outcome): Met. Section 1 states what the business gains before it names any technology. Item 2 (who the stakeholders are): Met. Section 1 lists 8 stakeholder groups. Item 3 (questions whose answers reshape the design): Met by the interview tree of six questions in Section 2. Item 4 (splitting and ranking requirements): Met. Section 2 keeps must-have functional needs apart from non-functional targets that can be measured. Item 5 (what is out of scope): Met. Section 2 names five things the MVP (minimum viable product) leaves out. Phase 2: Estimation & Architecture Item 6 (rough sizing and capacity arithmetic): Met. Section 3 runs a worked estimate, a four-step envelope and a sensitivity table. Item 7 (cost per unit, split by driver): Partly met. Section 3 lists cost per validated version among its SLO (service level objective) dimensions, yet no table separates cost into its drivers. Item 8 (the whole architecture and how data moves through it): Met. Section 4 gives the architecture diagram, a table of components and a sequence diagram. Item 9 (records and API contracts): Met. Section 5 specifies the four records and the four API contracts, and each contract states its auth, idempotency and error codes. Item 10 (whether to build or buy, and which vendor or model): Not met. The guide compares configuration with code and core with adapters, but never weighs vendors or BPM products against each other. Phase 3: Trade-offs, Security & Reliability Item 11 (named trade-offs, each with a fair verdict): Met by the four pairs in Section 8. Item 12 (threats and the controls that answer them): Met by Section 6, which sets out four security controls. Item 13 (drills for failure modes and reliability): Met. Section 6 runs a loop drill in four parts, four more failure cases and a policy table with six rows. Item 14 (how the system is tested): Met. sections.title: Key Takeaways
sections.text: Key Takeaways Reframe "configuration" as the outcome: one stable product core with customisation that is safe, versioned and supportable, so ten customers never become ten forks. Measure how often a new customer variation ships with no fork, no hotfix and no support escalation, not how many fields are configurable. Who writes the configuration is an architecture question, because customer admins need validation, previews, narrow building blocks and safe defaults. Size for the peak: 1,000 config versions a day is about 42 an hour, but half of them inside a 2-hour window is about 250 an hour before retries. Keep validation out of the save API, so save stays fast and durable, validation is queued and bounded, and deployment is idempotent and retryable. Deployment capacity is set by fan-out across tenants, regions and integrations, not by the number of human edits. Split the control plane, where configs are written, checked, versioned and promoted, from the data plane that runs live workflows, so risky change stays off the hot path. Publishing an immutable version does not switch it on: a tenant flag exposes it to one tenant, then a cohort, and rollback flips the flag back to the previous version. The append-only ConfigDeployment ledger, not the config record, says which version is live, so a rollback is a new event and never an edit in place. Publish runs parse, validate, authorise-by-policy, persist in that order, so cheap structural checks fail fast and nothing is written until every check passes. Create-style calls carry an idempotency key: the same key and body return the same deployment, a changed body gets 422 and a retry still in flight gets 409. Arbitrary code is off by default, and any approved extension runs in a sandbox with least privilege, resource caps and limits on outbound traffic. An infinite approval loop is caught by cycle detection at publish or a max-hop guard at runtime, and fails closed for that version while the tenant falls back to the last known-good one. Partition by tenant ID so one tenant's approval surge stays in its partition; at 100 times the baseline that becomes per-tenant quotas and sharded queues. Widen the configuration surface only after a second and third customer reuse the same mechanism, and steer by fork count and upgrade time per tenant.

sections.title: Level calibration
sections.text: Level calibrationOn a shared workflow platform for ten customers, the levels separate on how far the answer goes past "make it configurable". Level Sounds like Missing Senior "One workflow runtime, declarative configs in a versioned registry, a validator on publish and an adapter SDK for integrations. Save stays fast while validation and deployment run queued and idempotent, and an approval loop fails closed for that version." Who authors and approves configs, how a new version reaches one tenant before the rest, and who owns rollback. Staff "Split the control plane from the data plane: publish immutable versions, expose them behind a tenant flag and gate on the tenant test harness. Ownership is explicit: product owns templates, customers own values, integrations own adapters, ops own the ConfigDeployment ledger, and rollout starts with one willing customer admin." Which variations earn a place in core, how old schema generations retire, and whether to build the engine at all. Principal "Pick the workflow family the company wants to own and promote a capability to core only when its leverage is proven. Build the constrained configuration model, buy commodity pieces like identity federation, and run a deprecation policy with a small number of supported generations. Fork count and upgrade time per tenant are what the organisation steers by." Which differences recur, and what upgrade promise customers expect, need the first customers' real change requests to settle.

sections.title: Strong discovery questions
sections.text: Strong discovery questions Across the ten customers, which differences keep coming back and which happen only once? The first kind earns a platform capability; the second goes down an exception path. Is the variation limited to fields, approvals, branding and integrations? Or does it reach into business logic and the states a workflow can pass through? Who writes the configuration: our engineers, the customer's admins, or both, with the vendor signing off before anything reaches production? Which integrations must exist on day one? If an adapter fails, does the transition stop, or does the workflow carry on in a reduced mode? What do customers expect from an upgrade? Must their configs keep working, unchanged, through every core release? Where does custom code stop? Is it allowed in the trusted core, confined to a sandbox, or limited to integration points we have approved? How fast must a new customer be configured? A target of hours means self-service tooling. A target of a week leaves room for manual review. What should happen when someone misconfigures a workflow? Do we need a fallback approval path that always works?

  • Where does custom code stop? Is it allowed in the trusted core, confined to a sandbox, or limited to integration points we have approved?
  • How fast must a new customer be configured? A target of hours means self-service tooling. A target of a week leaves room for manual review.
  • What should happen when someone misconfigures a workflow? Do we need a fallback approval path that always works?

sections.title: Strong non-functional requirements
sections.text: Strong non-functional requirements Latency: split the budget by action. A save should feel instant, a validation preview may take a moment, and a full deployment can run slower as long as it is reliable. Availability: this case assumes about 1,000 configuration versions a day, with peaks at 3x. Validation and deployment therefore need separate paths, not one synchronous chain. Security: arbitrary code stays off unless explicitly allowed. Adapters and secrets belong to one tenant each. We also check the validation rules themselves, because a rule can be a denial-of-service risk. Compliance: keep a lasting record of who published each change, what it altered, which approval gate it passed and which version went live. Reliability: isolate configuration by tenant. A setting or test change from one tenant must never change how another tenant's workflows run. Cost: track spend per validated version and per activated template. Include the support load that a very flexible primitive brings with it.

sections.title: Architecture explanation
sections.text: Architecture explanation Configuration truth lives in the control plane, and workflows execute in the data plane. That separation stops the product splitting into ten forks. For every tenant, the workflow runtime handles instances, step transitions, timers and retries the same way. Published config versions are immutable. The configuration registry stores them with their release metadata and acts as the system of record. On every save and publish, the schema and rule validator runs synchronously. Syntax, semantic constraints, permissions and compatibility all get checked there. The UI renderer builds each tenant's forms, labels and layouts from the approved config. Apart from a cache, it stores nothing. CRM (customer relationship management), ERP (enterprise resource planning), ticketing and webhook connectors all sit behind one standard interface, the integration adapter SDK. Each tenant's credentials are held by reference. Rollout runs through a feature flag service, by tenant, cohort or percentage. The few extensions we approve run in a sandbox with strict limits. The migration service moves older configs onto new schema versions. Before a release ships, the tenant test harness replays each tenant's contract tests as a gate.

sections.title: Data model / integration assumptions
sections.text: Data model / integration assumptions WorkflowTemplate(id, engine_version, schema); TenantConfig(tenant_id, template_id, version, values); AdapterDefinition(name, contract_version, permissions); ConfigDeployment(tenant_id, version, state). ConfigDeployment acts as the deployment ledger. It is the source of truth for the draft, validated, deployed, rolled_back and failed states. A rollback adds a new deployment state. It never edits the earlier record, so we can always rebuild the full history. Each write states the version it expects to replace. Two operators racing on the same config then cannot overwrite each other without noticing. We tag every validation, deployment, adapter test and rollback with the tenant, the config version, a request ID and an idempotency key.

sections.title: Red-team risks
sections.text: Red-team risks approval loops that never end, drift in adapter contracts, upgrades that break old field mappings, flag combinations nobody tested, escape from the sandbox An approval graph with a cycle in it keeps looping at runtime. The harm is deterministic, so a retry will not fix it. A downstream service renames a field or changes its response shape. That adapter contract drift breaks every tenant on the adapter at the same moment. A tenant upgrade breaks old field mappings, and integrations still pointing at the previous version are left stranded. Two feature flags are each safe alone, but nobody tested them together, and the combination opens a bad path. Customer-defined logic escapes the sandbox. That is why arbitrary code is denied by default instead of only reviewed.

sections.title: Rollout plan
sections.text: Rollout plan Week 0-1: find out which differences recur, who owns the configuration and where the line for custom code falls. Week 1-2: show that one recurring pattern fits into shared primitives, with no one-off fork needed. Week 2-3: keep the gate closed until the team agrees that this pattern is stable enough to become a platform capability. Week 3-4: have the first customer admin configure their own workflow, then run a pilot through the real support channel. Week 5: before going wider, check that the customer accepts both the support model and the rollback procedure. Week 6-8: record a baseline for launch speed, defects and validation failures; scope grows only after that. After pilot: grow only if configuration is clearly cutting custom work, not hiding rework somewhere else.

sections.title: Final 2-minute spoken answer
sections.text: Final 2-minute spoken answerI wouldn't open with a list of features. People agree on the headline request and disagree on everything beneath it. So my first job is to pull apart what they asked for, configuration, from what the business needs: ten customers served without the product splitting into ten incompatible forks. I'd make that outcome testable with three words. Safe: no change skips authorisation or creates runtime behaviour nobody reviewed. Versioned: each customer knows which definition is live and what changed in it. Supportable: someone can diagnose a problem and roll a bad configuration back. My own scorecard counts the new customer variations that go live and never needed a fork, a hotfix or a call to support. A count of configurable fields would be a vanity number. The first real design choice is which differences recur. A difference in the approval chain that keeps coming back should become a platform capability. A single seasonal override belongs on an exception path. For the architecture, every tenant shares a single stable engine and a single release train. Declarative schemas carry most of the variation, and an adapter interface handles integrations. Configs are immutable and versioned, and we validate them before publish. A narrow sandbox exists only where declarative config can't go. Arbitrary code is off by default. Adapters and secrets belong to one tenant each, and we check validation rules too, in case one exhausts resources. The failure I'd name is an infinite approval loop. That version fails closed instead of carrying on. My first step is to show one recurring pattern working, and then a real customer admin pilots it.
